page.text:
Disjunction represents the logical 'or', written $P \lor Q$. In natural
language, the word 'or' is notoriously ambiguous: a menu offering 'soup
or salad' implies an exclusive choice, whereas a job requirement stating
'applicants must speak French or German' clearly welcomes applicants who
speak both.

Mathematics resolves this ambiguity decisively: unless explicitly
qualified, the mathematical connective $\lor$ is always *inclusive*. The
statement $P \lor Q$ is true when $P$ is true, when $Q$ is true, or when
both are true; it fails only when both $P$ and $Q$ are false. This
inclusive convention is indispensable in mathematical reasoning. For
example, the theorem stating that for every real number $x$, either
$x \ge 0$ or $x \le 0$, is valid without awkward qualifications for
$x = 0$ precisely because the connective permits both alternatives to
hold at once.
